blocks.content: Priority scheduling is a direct generalization of Shortest Job First. Instead of always favoring whichever process has the shortest burst time, it favors whatever the system decides matters most right now, and that could be burst time, but far more often it is something else entirely, such as how important a process is to the user or to the system itself.

This chapter explains the algorithm itself, the preemptive and non-preemptive variants, a full worked numeric example, how priorities actually get assigned in real systems, the starvation problem that follows directly from the algorithm's own logic, aging as the standard fix, the exact connection back to Shortest Job First, and how to talk about all of this cleanly in an interview.
1. The Algorithm: Choosing by Importance, Not Just Duration
blocks.text: 1. The Algorithm: Choosing by Importance, Not Just Duration

blocks.content: In priority scheduling every process in the system is assigned a priority, usually a small integer. Whenever the CPU becomes free, the scheduler looks at every process currently sitting in the ready queue and picks the one with the highest priority to run next. Everything else about the algorithm, how ties are broken, whether a running process can be interrupted, how priorities are chosen in the first place, is a design decision layered on top of this one simple rule: the highest priority ready process runs next.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: Priority scheduling always picks the ready process the system currently considers most important, not necessarily the one that will finish fastest.
2. Two Conventions: Lower Number or Higher Number
blocks.text: 2. Two Conventions: Lower Number or Higher Number

blocks.content: There is one detail about priority scheduling that catches almost everyone off guard the first time they meet it: which number actually counts as the highest priority. Some systems use the priority number directly, so a priority of ten beats a priority of five, and the largest number wins. Other systems flip this around completely and treat the number as a rank, where a smaller number means a more urgent process. Linux is a well known example of the second style: its nice values run from negative twenty, the most favorable, up to positive nineteen, the least favorable, so a lower nice value actually means the process gets more CPU attention, the opposite of what the word priority might suggest at first glance.

["Higher number wins: many textbook examples and some job scheduling systems treat a bigger priority number as more important, so priority 9 beats priority 2.","Lower number wins: Linux nice values, several real time operating systems, and many classic scheduler implementations treat a smaller number as more urgent, so priority 0 beats priority 9."]
items: Higher number wins: many textbook examples and some job scheduling systems treat a bigger priority number as more important, so priority 9 beats priority 2.
Lower number wins: Linux nice values, several real time operating systems, and many classic scheduler implementations treat a smaller number as more urgent, so priority 0 beats priority 9.

blocks.title: Always check, never assume
blocks.content: There is no universal rule here, and getting it backwards is a genuinely common source of bugs and confusion. Before reading or writing any priority based scheduling code, confirm which convention the specific system uses. Do not assume it just because a similar system worked a certain way.
3. Preemptive and Non-preemptive Priority Scheduling
Preemptive priority scheduling

In the preemptive version, the scheduler is always watching. If a new process arrives in the ready queue with a higher priority than the process currently running on the CPU, the running process is immediately paused and moved back into the ready queue, and the new arrival takes over the CPU right away. The process that was running does not get to finish its current burst first, it simply loses the CPU the moment something more important shows up.
Non-preemptive priority scheduling

In the non-preemptive version, once a process is given the CPU it keeps it until that process finishes its burst or voluntarily gives up the CPU, no matter what arrives in the meantime. A newly arrived process, even one with a far higher priority than whatever is currently running, has to wait in the ready queue. It only becomes eligible to be picked once the CPU is actually free again.

blocks.title: Which one matters more
blocks.content: Preemptive priority scheduling reacts faster to important new work but adds the overhead and complexity of context switches at unpredictable moments. Non-preemptive priority scheduling is simpler to implement and reason about, but a long low priority burst can block an urgent process for its entire remaining duration once that burst has already started.
4. A Worked Example

Numbers make this concrete faster than any amount of prose. Consider four processes arriving at different times, each carrying its own priority. For this example we will use the convention where a lower number means a higher priority, the same convention Linux uses for nice values, and we will schedule them non-preemptively.
{"headers":["Process","Arrival Time","Burst Time","Priority (lower number wins)"],"rows":[["P1","0","4","2"],["P2","1","3","1"],["P3","2","1","3"],["P4","3","5","4"]]}

At time 0 only P1 has arrived, so it starts running immediately, and because this is non-preemptive scheduling it runs all the way to completion regardless of who arrives while it is running. By the time P1 finishes at time 4, P2, P3, and P4 have all already arrived and are waiting in the ready queue. Among them P2 has the best priority, so it runs next, from time 4 to time 7. When P2 finishes, P3 and P4 remain, and P3 has the better priority, so it runs from time 7 to time 8. Only P4 is left at that point, and it finally runs from time 8 to time 13.

blocks.title: Average waiting time
blocks.content: Adding up the four waiting times, 0, 3, 5, and 5, and dividing by 4 gives an average waiting time of 3.25 units. Notice that P4 arrived only one unit after P1 but ends up with a turnaround time of 10 units, purely because it drew the lowest priority. That is priority scheduling working exactly as designed, and also a preview of the problem covered next.
5. How Priorities Are Assigned in Real Systems
blocks.text: 5. How Priorities Are Assigned in Real Systems

blocks.content: Static priorities

A static priority is fixed for the entire lifetime of a process and never changes on its own. It is typically assigned at creation time based on what kind of process it is. A core system process that manages hardware might automatically get a high static priority, while an ordinary user application gets a lower one. An administrator can also assign or override a static priority directly, for example marking a backup job as low priority so it never interferes with interactive work.
Dynamic priorities

A dynamic priority is recalculated automatically while the process runs, based on its observed behavior. A common rule of thumb rewards processes that use a lot of input and output but very little CPU, since that pattern usually means the process is interactive, like a text editor waiting on keystrokes, and boosting its priority makes the whole system feel more responsive to a human sitting in front of it. A process that continuously burns CPU with little or no I/O looks batch like or computational, and its priority is often nudged downward over time.

["System process: kernel threads and device handlers are typically given the highest static priority, since the whole machine depends on them.","Interactive user process: often starts at a moderate priority and gets boosted dynamically if it behaves in an I/O heavy, bursty way.","Background batch job: often started with, or decays toward, a low priority since nothing is waiting on it directly."]
items: System process: kernel threads and device handlers are typically given the highest static priority, since the whole machine depends on them.
Interactive user process: often starts at a moderate priority and gets boosted dynamically if it behaves in an I/O heavy, bursty way.
Background batch job: often started with, or decays toward, a low priority since nothing is waiting on it directly.

blocks.content: 6. Starvation: The Serious Flaw

Priority scheduling has one serious, well documented flaw: starvation. If a steady stream of higher priority processes keeps arriving, a low priority process can be skipped over indefinitely. Every time the scheduler looks at the ready queue, something more important is sitting there, so the low priority process simply never gets picked. In principle it could wait forever, and on real systems under heavy, sustained load from higher priority work, this is not a rare edge case. It is a genuinely serious operational problem, not just a theoretical curiosity raised in a textbook.

A famous illustration comes from an old story about a mainframe at MIT: a low priority process sat waiting in the ready queue for years while a continuous stream of higher priority work kept cutting in front of it.

blocks.title: What starvation looks like in practice
blocks.content: Picture a shared print server that assigns high priority to urgent office documents and low priority to a large personal print job. If urgent documents keep arriving throughout the day, the personal job can sit in the queue untouched for hours, not because anything is broken, but because the scheduler is doing exactly what priority scheduling tells it to do.
7. Aging: The Standard Fix for Starvation
blocks.text: 7. Aging: The Standard Fix for Starvation

blocks.content: The standard, elegant fix for starvation is called aging. The idea is simple: the longer a process waits in the ready queue without running, the more its priority is gradually improved, until eventually even the lowest priority process in the system has waited long enough to outrank everything else and finally gets its turn on the CPU. Aging guarantees that no process can be skipped forever, because waiting itself becomes a form of currency that keeps accumulating.

To see the mechanism precisely it helps to work through actual numbers. For this example we will switch to the convention where a higher priority value is more favorable, just to show that aging works the same way no matter which convention a system uses, the scheduler always nudges the value in whichever direction counts as more favorable locally. Suppose process P5 arrives with a starting priority of just 1, the lowest in the system, while a continuous stream of other processes keep arriving with priority 8. The scheduler ages P5 by adding 1 point to its priority for every 3 time units it spends waiting without running.

{"headers":["Time Waited","P5 Priority Value","Status"],"rows":[["0","1","Waiting, far below the priority 8 arrivals"],["3","2","Waiting"],["6","3","Waiting"],["9","4","Waiting"],["12","5","Waiting"],["15","6","Waiting"],["18","7","Waiting, closing in"],["21","8","Now matches the arriving processes and finally runs"]]}

By the time P5 has waited 21 time units, its aged priority of 8 matches the priority of the processes that keep arriving, and it finally gets a turn on the CPU. Without aging, P5 could have been skipped indefinitely for as long as priority 8 work kept showing up. With aging, the wait is bounded: it is exactly the amount of time the aging formula takes to close the gap between where a process started and where it needed to be.
8. The Connection to Shortest Job First
blocks.text: 8. The Connection to Shortest Job First

blocks.content: There is a genuinely illuminating connection between priority scheduling and Shortest Job First that is worth stating precisely. If a system sets a process's priority equal to its burst time, and always favors the process with the numerically smallest value, exactly the lower number wins convention, then priority scheduling and Shortest Job First become the exact same algorithm. SJF is not a separate idea sitting next to priority scheduling, it is priority scheduling with one very specific, very narrow choice of what priority means: how long the process will run. Every property SJF has, including its own vulnerability to starvation when short jobs keep arriving, is really just a special case of a property priority scheduling already has.

blocks.title: The general pattern
blocks.content: Once you see priority scheduling as the general case and SJF as one particular choice of priority, a whole family of scheduling algorithms starts to look like variations on the same underlying rule: assign each process a number, and always run whichever one has the best number right now.
9. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle
blocks.text: 9. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle

blocks.content: Common mistakes

["Assuming the convention: treating a lower priority number as automatically worse, or automatically better, without checking how the specific system defines it, is one of the most common and easiest to avoid mistakes in this whole topic.","Forgetting aging entirely: writing or tracing through a scheduling simulation without any aging mechanism, then being surprised when a low priority process never runs in the trace, when that is in fact the algorithm working exactly as specified.","Ignoring the preemptive versus non-preemptive distinction: computing a schedule as if the CPU can be preempted when the question specifies a non-preemptive scheduler, or the reverse, changes every waiting time in the answer."]
items: Assuming the convention: treating a lower priority number as automatically worse, or automatically better, without checking how the specific system defines it, is one of the most common and easiest to avoid mistakes in this whole topic.

Forgetting aging entirely: writing or tracing through a scheduling simulation without any aging mechanism, then being surprised when a low priority process never runs in the trace, when that is in fact the algorithm working exactly as specified.

Ignoring the preemptive versus non-preemptive distinction: computing a schedule as if the CPU can be preempted when the question specifies a non-preemptive scheduler, or the reverse, changes every waiting time in the answer.

blocks.content: The interview angle

Interviewers like priority scheduling because it rewards precision. It is easy to state the rule, always run the highest priority ready process, but a strong answer also states the convention being used before computing anything, walks through a preemptive or non-preemptive trace correctly depending on what was asked, and, unprompted, brings up starvation and aging as the algorithm's central weakness and its standard fix. Mentioning that priority scheduling generalizes Shortest Job First, and being able to show exactly how, is the kind of detail that separates a memorized answer from a genuinely understood one.
